title: CELPIP General Listening — Practice Test 26
instructions: Listen to the audio for each part and answer the questions. Each audio plays once.

listeningScripts.title: Car Rental Damage Dispute
listeningScripts.text: Customer: I'm returning my rental car, and I want to dispute a damage claim you're making. Rental Agent: Okay, let me look into that. What's your rental agreement number? Customer: It's CR-892447. I rented the blue Hyundai Elantra, and there was already a dent on the back bumper when I picked it up. Agent: Let me check the pickup photos. What time did you pick up the vehicle? Customer: 10 AM on Tuesday, June 3rd. Agent: I found those photos. You're right, there is a dent visible in the corner of the back bumper. The damage report lists a scratch on the driver's door, which I don't see in our pickup images. Can you tell me what happened? Customer: I definitely didn't cause that scratch. I was careful the whole time I had it. Agent: When did you return the vehicle? Customer: Just now, at 4 PM today. Agent: And you purchased the damage waiver insurance at rental? Customer: Yes, I paid the extra $18 per day for that. Agent: Great. Since you purchased the damage waiver, any damage during your rental period, except for gross negligence, is covered. This scratch appears to be new damage, but with your waiver, you're not responsible. Customer: So I don't have to pay anything? Agent: Correct. Your coverage applies. The previous dent was there before you rented it, and this new scratch is covered under your damage waiver. You're all set.

listeningScripts.title: Roommate Household Discussion
listeningScripts.text: Alex: Hey, we need to talk about the dishes piling up in the sink. Jamie: Yeah, I know. I've been really busy with work this week. Alex: I get that, but it's been sitting there for three days. Jamie: I'm sorry, I'll do them tonight. Alex: Thanks. Also, we need to talk about the grocery situation. Jamie: What do you mean? Alex: I've been buying most of the groceries, and we're not splitting the cost fairly. Jamie: You're right. How do you want to handle it? Alex: We could split everything equally, or we could each buy our own stuff separately. Jamie: I think splitting equally makes more sense. We can keep a shared list. Alex: Great. One more thing—the internet bill is due next week. It's $75 this month. Jamie: That's higher than last month. Alex: Yeah, they increased the plan by five dollars. Jamie: Okay, so $37.50 each? Alex: Exactly. I'll send you a reminder.

listeningScripts.title: Public Transit New Route Announcement
listeningScripts.text: Good afternoon. Transit Authority is pleased to announce a new rapid bus route effective September 1st. The new Route 95 Express connects downtown to the northern suburbs, with stops at Central Station, City Hall, the Hospital, University Campus, and North Terminal. Service runs Monday through Friday from 6 AM to 10 PM, with departures every fifteen minutes during peak hours, 7 to 9 AM and 4 to 7 PM. Off-peak service is every thirty minutes. Weekend service begins December, with departures every twenty minutes from 9 AM to 8 PM. The Route 95 uses the new dedicated bus lane on Main Street, reducing travel time from downtown to North Terminal from forty-five minutes to approximately twenty-two minutes. Fares are the same as existing routes: single trip is three dollars fifty cents, and a monthly pass is ninety dollars. Seniors and students receive a twenty percent discount. The new buses feature USB charging ports, free Wi-Fi, and comfortable seating. Detailed schedules are available on our website and at all transit stations. Real-time tracking is available through our mobile app.

listeningScripts.title: Nova Scotia Healthcare Worker Recruitment
listeningScripts.text: Nova Scotia is launching an aggressive recruitment campaign to address critical shortages in healthcare professionals. The province has announced a 35 million dollar investment in recruitment and retention initiatives. Currently, there are over 800 unfilled nursing positions across Nova Scotia hospitals and clinics. The campaign targets nurses, physiotherapists, occupational therapists, and laboratory technicians. Starting salaries for nurses are being increased by 12 percent to compete with other provinces. The government is also offering signing bonuses of up to 15,000 dollars for candidates relocating to rural communities. Housing assistance programs will help new recruits find affordable accommodation. International recruitment is underway, with partnerships established with nursing programs in the Philippines and India. Officials estimate it will take approximately 18 months to fill 60 percent of the vacant positions. Patient wait times have increased significantly due to staffing shortages, with some emergency departments reporting delays of four to six hours.

listeningScripts.title: Workplace Safety Initiative
listeningScripts.text:
Safety Officer Tom: I've been analyzing our workplace incident reports from the past two years, and I'm concerned about our trend. We've had 34 reported injuries this year, which is up 15 percent from last year. Most incidents are slips, trips, and falls in warehouse areas. I'm proposing we implement mandatory safety training for all warehouse staff every six months, not annually as we currently do.

Warehouse Manager David: Tom, I appreciate your concern, but I'm worried about requiring training every six months. That's a lot of time away from work. My team's productivity is already under pressure with current targets. If we pull people off the floor for training frequently, we'll fall further behind on our goals. Can't we just focus on better signage and equipment?

Worker Representative Angela: I actually support Tom's proposal. I work in the warehouse, and I've seen some close calls that could have been serious. The issue isn't signage—we know the hazards. The problem is we get complacent. Regular training keeps safety top of mind. Plus, Tom, I think twice-yearly training would actually improve morale because workers feel the company cares about their wellbeing.

Safety Officer Tom: Thank you, Angela. David, I understand your concern about productivity, but consider the cost of injuries. Each workplace injury costs us about $12,000 in direct and indirect costs. If we can prevent even three injuries per year, the training pays for itself. And research shows regular safety training actually reduces injuries, which ultimately improves productivity.

listeningScripts.title: Digital Privacy in the Workplace
listeningScripts.text: I want to talk about something that concerns me deeply—workplace monitoring and digital privacy. Many companies today monitor their employees constantly: they track keystrokes, monitor websites visited, log bathroom breaks through card access, and even use AI to analyze email and chat conversations. The argument is usually that this improves productivity and security, but I think it's gone too far. Yes, employers have legitimate security concerns, but the level of surveillance we're accepting is unprecedented. When employees feel constantly watched, it creates anxiety and erodes trust. Studies show that excessive monitoring actually decreases productivity and morale. Workers spend time trying to appear productive rather than actually being productive. Moreover, there's a moral issue here. As an employee, you're a person, not a machine to be optimized. You deserve privacy and dignity at work. I'm not arguing against all monitoring—reasonable security measures are necessary. But there's a middle ground between trusting employees completely and treating them like suspects. Companies that have implemented less invasive monitoring policies actually report higher employee satisfaction and retention. So my position is this: employers should use targeted monitoring only where necessary for genuine security reasons, not blanket surveillance of everything everyone does. Trust and respect for employee privacy create better workplaces.
